title: DoD Standard Internet Protocol
summary: A 1980 specification of the DoD Standard Internet Protocol, an early form of IP for moving datagrams across connected networks. It was replaced by RFC 791 and updated by RFC 777.

plainLanguage.summary: This is an early version of the rules for sending packets across networks, later replaced by the final version.

subtitle: The DoD Standard Internet Protocol specification from 1980, the predecessor to modern IP.

tldr.problem: In the 1970s, ARPA needed a protocol to move data packets across interconnected networks of different types, handling networks that could lose, reorder, or duplicate packets.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 760 specifies the Internet Protocol (IP), which adds a header to data to carry source and destination addresses, handles fragmentation for small-packet networks, includes a checksum, and provides options like priority, time-to-live, and special routing.
tldr.outcome: IP became the foundation of the Internet, though this 1980 version was updated by RFC 791 which is the standard still in use today.

today: RFC 760 is historic and was replaced by RFC 791. It was also updated by RFC 777. The basic concepts of IP remain the same in modern IPv4.

sections.title: What IP Does
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol (IP) solves the problem of sending data across a "catenet" - a system of many interconnected packet-switched networks. It adds a header to data so routers can forward packets based on destination addresses. IP is connectionless: each datagram is independent, not part of a stream or virtual circuit.

IP handles two fundamental tasks: addressing (using fixed-length addresses to identify source and destination hosts) and fragmentation (breaking large datagrams into smaller pieces for networks that cannot handle them, then reassembling at the destination). IP does not guarantee delivery, order, or duplicate prevention - it relies on higher-layer protocols like TCP for those services.
sections.plainLanguage: IP is a mail service for computer packets. It puts on an address label and sends each packet independently. Big packets get cut into pieces if needed.

sections.title: The IP Header
sections.content:
The IP header is at least 20 bytes (5 words of 32 bits each). Key fields include Version (4 bits, set to 4 for IPv4), Internet Header Length (4 bits, stating the header size), Type of Service (8 bits, for priority and quality hints), Total Length (16 bits, the datagram size), Identification (16 bits, grouping fragments), Flags (3 bits, including the more-fragments flag), Fragment Offset (13 bits, positioning fragments), Time to Live (8 bits, a hop count to prevent looping), Protocol (8 bits, identifying the next protocol), Header Checksum (16 bits), and 32-bit Source and Destination addresses.

Optional fields for routing, timestamps, and error reports can follow. The header is padded to a 32-bit boundary.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a postal label that says where it came from, where it is going, how big it is, and how far it can travel before being thrown away.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
sections.content: When an IP datagram is too large for a network, routers fragment it. Each fragment keeps the same Identification field and Source and Destination addresses, and includes a Fragment Offset indicating its position in the original datagram. The more-fragments flag is set for all fragments except the last. The receiving end collects fragments by matching these four fields and uses the offset to place each piece in the right position.
sections.plainLanguage: A big box that does not fit on the truck gets broken into smaller boxes. Each box is labeled with which big box it came from and its position. At the destination, they are taped back together.

sections.title: Design Choices
sections.content:
IP includes several key features. Type of Service indicates quality hints (interactive vs. bulk vs. real-time traffic). Time to Live acts as a self-destruct timer, decremented at each hop and discarding the datagram if it reaches zero, preventing loops. The Options field provides optional control like timestamps and error reporting. The Header Checksum protects against transmission errors only in the header, not the data - higher-layer protocols handle data integrity.

Notably, IP provides no acknowledgments, flow control, or data error correction. These are the job of protocols like TCP that sit above IP.
sections.plainLanguage: IP is simple: send packets and hope they get there. TCP, above it, handles retrying if something goes wrong.

fields.name: Total Length
fields.desc: Datagram length including header and data

fields.name: Identification
fields.desc: Groups fragments of the same datagram

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: More Fragments and other control bits

fields.name: Fragment Offset
fields.desc: Position of this fragment in the datagram

fields.name: Protocol
fields.desc: Identifies the next protocol (TCP, UDP, etc)

fields.name: Header Checksum
fields.desc: One's complement checksum of the header
